newsitem.title: USA: Healthy bank industry sees low fees for insurance.
newsitem.headline: Healthy bank industry sees low fees for insurance.

text.p: Most banks and savings institutions will not have to pay for deposit insurance coverage in the second half of 1997, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. decided on Tuesday.

Thanks to the continued low number of bank failures and a successful recapitalization of the insurance funds last year, about 95 percent of banks and 90 percent of savings institutions will not be assessed insurance premiums, the agency said.
The agency's board of directors approved a sliding scale of insurance assessments ranging from zero to 0.27 percent of deposits, with healthy institutions paying less.
Banks and thrifts paid special one-time assessments of $4.7 billion under a law passed by Congress last year to revive the savings industry's depleted fund.
By the end of 1996, the savings insurance fund stood at $8.89 billion, or 1.3 percent of insured savings deposits. By law, the coverage ratio must be at least 1.25 percent.

Fred Carns, assistant director of the FDIC, said even with most thrifts exempt from paying for insurance, the savings fund would end the year with between $9.29 billion to $9.40 billion and a coverage ratio between 1.31 percent and 1.43 percent.

The bank fund, which ended 1996 at $26.85 billion, is projected to rise to between $27.16 billion and $27.86 billion, Carns said. The coverage ratio should rise from 1.34 percent to as high as 1.42 percent, he said.

"Essentially by virtue of the fact that the (fund) is capitalised and there are low losses, interest earnings are enough to add to the ratio even with 95 percent of the industry paying zero," FDIC Chairwoman Ricki Helfer said at the board meeting.
Banks had record earnings of $52.4 billion last year and only six federally insured institutions failed, the lowest total since 1972.
Analysts said the outlook for the industry remained extremely positive.
"Bank failures are few and far between," said Tom Theurkauf, senior vice president at Keefe, Bruyette & Woods. "It's a healthy outlook."
Bank losses on credit cards have been mounting recently, but the situation is unlikely to cause serious problems, Theurkauf said.

"If there's a fly in the ointment it is on consumer debt and specifically credit cards. But I think at the end of the day, we'll find that a very manageable situation for the vast majority of banks," he said.
